newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia eyes measures to curb rebel onslaught.
newsitem.headline: Colombia eyes measures to curb rebel onslaught.

text.p: President Ernesto Samper huddled with his military chiefs, top cabinet officials and state governors on Tuesday to discuss ways of stemming a recent surge in leftist guerrilla activity across Colombia.

The meeting at the ornate Casa de Narino presidential palace in downtown Bogota, dubbed a "law and order summit" by Samper's official spokesman, comes against the backdrop of a rebel offensive beginning in late August that killed more than 150 security force members and wounded hundreds.

Guerrillas also took more than 60 soldiers prisoner, blew up oil pipelines and paralysed key roadways, burning trucks and blocking exports of coal, coffee in a spiral of attacks that caused tens of millions of dollars in economic losses.

Adding to widpesread fears that the security situation threatens to spin out of control, authorities said on Friday that they had uncovered rebel plans to launch a series of high-profile attacks in Bogota as part of a guerrilla effort to move their war from the countryside to the streets of the capital.
Strategic rebel targets included the presidential palace and the fortress-like U.S. embassy compound, Defence Minister Juan Carlos Esguerra told reporters.

Government officials have said they were considering calling up Colombia's military reserves to confront what many agree to be the most dramatic offensive Colombia has seen in more than three decades of guerrilla war.

No one has said where the cash-strapped government would come up with the money for additional military financing this year, however, and that may be one of the issues Samper put on the agenda for Tuesday's talks with Esguerra, Interior Minister Horacio Serpa, senior military officials and governors from provinces that have been hardest hit by recent and emboldened rebel activity.

Guerrillas have fought under the banner of land reform for decades and El Tiempo, Colombia's leading newspaper, said the government is preparing to order the expropriation of large land holdings -- and their handover to landless peasants -- in areas torn by political bloodshed.

Alvaro Uribe, governor of northwestern Antioquia province, told reporters on his arrival at the presidential palace that he knew nothing about possible agrarian reform aimed at easing peasant unrest, however.
Antioquia, where gunmen of the left and right have killed with impunity for decades, is one of the provinces that have suffered the most during Colombia's prolonged guerrilla war.

Four National Liberation Army (ELN) guerrillas were killed in fighting in a rural area of the province early on Tuesday. Military spokesmen said the dead included Humberto Manuel Mesa Lopera, a rebel commando linked to the killing of two small town mayors and a string of kidnappings and extortion rackets in Antioquia.

Three other rebels were killed in fighting elsewhere across the country on Tuesday, including two gunned down in a firefight with the military in central Cundinamarca, the province that rings the capital.

Interior Minister Serpa, in brief remarks to reporters during a recess in the closed-door meeting at the presidential palace, conceded that guerrillas have wreaked havoc across the country since late August.
He ruled out any dramatic measures such as the declaration of a state of emergency, however, saying the public order situation appeared to be on the mend.
"The authorities have effective control over all areas of the country," he said. "We hope that the situation will continue improving in the immediate future."
